The bedug is a membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.212.1, a large double-headed drum with buffalo or cow hide at both ends fixed by pegs, whose pitch cannot be adjusted. It is hung in a frame, struck with soft mallets, and often played with a rhythm that gets faster and faster. It appears in gamelan, but mostly in special ensembles such as the Yogyakarta kendang style and sekaten, and also plays with the kendang to accompany dance. In the mosques of Indonesia and Malaysia the Javanese and Sundanese strike it before the call to prayer to mark prayer times, and it is also used during Ramadan and on the eve of Idul Fitri.

貝杜格鼓的使用脈絡見於印尼與馬來群島的甘美蘭及清真寺傳統。在爪哇，爪哇族與巽他族: The bedug's context lies in the gamelan and mosque traditions of Indonesia and the Malay Archipelago. In Java the Javanese and Sundanese use it to give the prayer signal before the call to prayer or on Islamic holidays; during Ramadan it can mark the end of the day's fast and sometimes the pre-dawn meal, and Friday prayer has its own stroke. In special ensembles it can replace the kempul in sekaten gamelan, and some Yogyakarta kendang styles use it too, alongside the kendang, to accompany dance. The tradition is also found among the Malays of Sarawak, who call it tetel, and among the Maranao Muslims of the southern Philippines, who announce prayer times on a smaller similar drum, the tabu or tabo.
